justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 297.5 for the one-day horizon and gradually rising to 303.0 at one month. This drift assumption is grounded in the general historical tendency of equity markets to trend slightly upward over time, combined with a baseline assumption that no major negative catalyst is imminent. The one-day estimate anchors closely to the current price level, as short-term mean reversion and inertia tend to dominate over very brief windows. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, I incorporated a small positive drift premium reflecting expected risk compensation, while also acknowledging that mean-reversion forces weaken and trend or momentum factors can compound over longer periods.

The confidence interval widths grow systematically with time horizon, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that is standard in financial modeling. For the one-day window, the 19-point spread is relatively tight because overnight and intraday volatility, while real, is bounded in normal conditions. By one week, the interval widens to 34 points, capturing the accumulation of daily shocks as well as the possibility of mid-week macro data releases or central bank communications. At one month, the 70-point spread reflects the substantial uncertainty introduced by earnings seasons, geopolitical developments, and shifts in monetary policy expectations, all of which can materially reprice assets over a four-week window. Implied volatility levels and recent realized volatility in the underlying instrument also informed my scaling of these intervals.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data such as a significant miss on employment or inflation figures could trigger sharp repricing, especially if it alters Federal Reserve rate expectations abruptly. A geopolitical shock, credit event, or liquidity stress in a correlated market could also produce tail outcomes well below my lower bound. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from major central banks, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, or a sudden resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could drive prices above my upper bounds. These fat-tail events are not fully captured by symmetric Gaussian-style intervals, meaning the true distribution likely has heavier tails than my confidence intervals imply, particularly at the one-month horizon where the opportunity for compounding surprises is greatest.
